A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Alignment Score framework and reasoning-chain selection research, despite the changed title and substantial revision. The text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: Section 4 and Tables 1–5 report original model evaluations, reasoning-error measurements, regression analysis, and SCOS selection results.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendices E–F report original accuracy and alignment measurements, judge/backbone comparisons, and qualitative case studies.

M1.justification: The scoring algorithm switches from KL to Jensen–Shannon divergence. The SCOS error-based selectors become ACSS variants, with redundancy detection revised from consecutive exact duplicates to semantic overlap with any earlier step. v2 also introduces direct score maximization through ACSS-Ali. and majority-answer filtering followed by alignment-based selection through SC-Align.

E1.justification: ScienceQA-only evaluation becomes a mixture of text-only ScienceQA and ARC-Challenge, and reasoning coverage extends from 1–3 hops to 1–4 hops. Benchmark-score comparisons also replace TruthfulQA, GSM8K, and HellaSwag with MATH and GPQA while retaining MMLU.

E2.justification: Standard CoT and SC-CoT remain the designated baselines in the corresponding selection experiments (v1 Table 4; v2 Table 2). The additional ACSS-Ali. and SC-Align rows expand the proposed method family; no additional baseline algorithm is introduced.

E3.justification: The evaluation changes from 1,000 sampled questions to 1,024 mixed-dataset questions with 256 reference chains per hop, substantially revises the evaluated model roster, and changes the alignment metric. The prompt now requires JSON, default single-sample temperature changes from 0.7 to 0.4, and TS thresholds become development-set calibrated. New judge evaluations introduce 1–10 ratings and randomized candidate order.

E4.justification: v1's four-error analysis and least-squares decomposition are removed, with v2 retaining revised TS/RR analyses across four depths. v2 adds NLI-backbone robustness comparisons and a three-judge by three-backbone grid ablation. Appendix F introduces four selector-comparison cases, including a failure case, replacing v1 Appendix B's GPT-3.5-versus-GPT-4 discussion.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without a repeated-run or seed protocol. v2 states that every configuration, including ablations, uses five independent seeded runs and introduces mean±standard-deviation reporting and error bars. This establishes a substantial reporting change, not an increase from a known earlier run count.

E6.justification: Most result entries are replaced under changed metrics, data, and model configurations, preventing interpretation as same-setting gains. v2 adds accuracy and judge ratings; Table 3 reports ACSS-Ali. gains of 0.57 percentage points in accuracy and 7.99 alignment points over SC-CoT. The earlier universal 2-hop peak now has a GPT-4o-mini exception: 81.58 at 1-hop versus 80.66 at 2-hop.

T1.justification: v2 replaces the formal KL-based divergence with a symmetric JS definition and revises RR's mathematical criterion. It removes v1's weighted four-error decomposition and the logical-disconnection and causal-reversal definitions (v1 Equations 6–10; v2 Equations 4–6). These change the mathematical formulation, not merely its notation.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion shift emphasis from SCOS improving alignment by 29.84% and explaining four error types to Alignment Score diagnosing task correctness and human-preferred reasoning. ACSS and SC-Align replace SCOS as named contributions. The central observation of a 2-hop alignment peak is retained.

C2.justification: The regression-based explanation of 2-hop superiority is replaced by an argument about 1-hop structural degeneracy and error accumulation across increasing pairwise relations. v2 adds interpretations of accuracy coupling and judge/backbone stability. Its new Limitations section identifies dependence on explicitly separated steps, untested transfer beyond multiple-choice QA, and the absence of a formal account of depth-related degradation.

D1.justification: Appendices A–D add detailed system/user and judge prompts, JSON schemas, top-p and token limits, threshold calibration, and AI-assisted reference curation with human spot-checks. Model-version dates and GPU memory are also specified. However, v1 Appendix C's explicit budget of ten candidate chains per question is no longer specified in v2.

R1.justification: Related work shifts from surveys of test-time reasoning strategies and reasoning errors toward semantic uncertainty and structured evaluation. v2 adds substantial discussion of semantic entropy, Kernel Language Entropy, Shapley Uncertainty, and Semantic Energy, plus LLM-as-judge literature, while removing the earlier ToT/FoT/GoT/Buffer-of-Thought positioning.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, RQ3 narrative, and conclusion are substantially rewritten around structured alignment evaluation. Method subsections are reorganized, a Limitations section is added, and the appendices are restructured from A–C into A–F, with retained experimental details redistributed.

P2.justification: Figures 1–2 are redrawn, with the pipeline figure adding reference preparation. The four-error illustration disappears and new hop-score and error-rate plots appear. Benchmark and depth results are combined into one table, the selection table gains accuracy/alignment sections and color coding, and the appendices add threshold and judge-grid tables.

improvement.justification: Bounded JS scoring, richer documentation, five-run summaries, and new accuracy/robustness checks address important weaknesses of v1. However, v2's new 1-hop explanation implies identical normalized one-point distributions, which should yield a score of 100, unlike Table 1. Its positive control-group example in Appendix F also rewards a conclusion contradicting the preceding steps. These inconsistencies affect the newly emphasized validation and interpretation, leaving the net quality change uncertain.
